query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid quenching during synthesis will stabilize a dual-phase microstructure in FeCoNiTi alloys in which the coexistence of a ferromagnetic fcc phase and a hexagonal C14 Laves phase promotes a substantial increase in coercivity via spin-canted domain wall pinning.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast high-entropy alloy FeCoNiTi (nominal 1:1:1:1) containing dual phases: fcc and hexagonal C14 Laves.
generation.intervention: Apply rapid quenching (using arc melting on a water-cooled copper hearth) to lock in the dual-phase microstructure and compare against a compositionally matched C14-dominant variant (Fe27Co27Ni17Ti29).
generation.conditions: Magnetic measurements performed up to 400 K with corresponding electronic structure assessments via spin-polarized density of states calculations.
generation.structural_mediator: The chemically segregated coexistence of an fcc phase (approximately 21.3Fe-24.8Co-32.2Ni-21.6Ti) and a C14 Laves phase (approximately 27.3Fe-26.6Co-17.4Ni-28.7Ti) mediates interphase interactions.
generation.mechanism: Antiferromagnetic coupling between the Fe/Co/Ni sublattice and the Ti sublattice in the dual-phase system reduces overall saturation magnetization but enhances domain wall pinning through a boosted orbital moment effect in the fcc phase. This robust interphase interaction triggers a high-temperature ferromagnetic ordering (1084 K) in the fcc phase and introduces additional magnetic transitions (e.g., 168 K), collectively leading to an elevated coercive field.
generation.predicted_outcome: The dual-phase alloy’s fcc component will exhibit a coercive field significantly higher than the 100 Oe seen in single-phase fcc alloys, with measured values approaching approximately 667 Oe at 400 K, and display a set of distinct magnetic ordering transitions differentiable from those of the C14 phase.
generation.baseline: Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloys and related derivatives that display coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe with limited orbital moment contribution.
generation.boundary: The observed behavioral enhancement depends on the interphase interactions between the fcc and C14 Laves phases; pure single-phase fcc or pure C14 alloys will not exhibit the same high coercivity or multi-transition magnetic profile.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact quantitative magnitude of the increase in coercivity and the precise field values at elevated temperatures, as these depend on the detailed kinetics of phase stabilization during rapid quenching.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: (1) the dual-phase FeCoNiTi prepared via rapid quenching and (2) a compositionally matched, C14-dominant variant (Fe27Co27Ni17Ti29). Perform magnetic measurements to observe the coercive fields and magnetic transition temperatures in both samples.
measurements: Measurement of coercive field values up to 400 K for both samples.
Identification of multiple magnetic ordering transitions (e.g., around 168 K, 214 K, and 1084 K) using magnetometry.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase alloy does not exhibit a coercive field significantly above 100 Oe—specifically, if it does not approach the predicted ~667 Oe at 400 K—or if the magnetic transition profile fails to show distinct transitions attributable to the fcc phase relative to the C14 dominant sample, then the hypothesis is rejected.
